claims.text: The target eutectic HEA contains a ductile matrix together with harder intermetallic or sigma phases that produce internal mechanical heterogeneity.
At elevated temperature, frictional heating promotes tribo-oxidation and formation of a protective oxide layer.
The in situ oxide layer is compositionally or structurally heterogeneous.
Differences in mechanical properties between the ductile and brittle eutectic phases concentrate stress at their interfaces.
Cyclic sliding stress can accumulate in and fragment or spall a protective oxide film.
Oxide spallation occurs preferentially at phase boundaries because of local strain mismatch.
Removal of the oxide film exposes fresh substrate regions.
Freshly exposed substrate regions undergo rapid corrosion in the corrosive environment.
Fragments generated by oxide-film breakup act as abrasive debris.
Abrasive oxide debris accelerates wear and material loss.
Loss of a lubricating glaze or oxide layer increases wear.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion cause synergistically greater total degradation than isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Under simultaneous exposure, the wear rate increases relative to the wear-only baseline.
Under simultaneous exposure, the corrosion rate increases relative to the corrosion-only baseline.
Wear-only or corrosion-only exposure at the same temperature produces a more stable oxide film than simultaneous exposure.
Temperatures at or above approximately 600 °C promote tribo-oxidation and thermal softening relevant to the proposed mechanism.
At lower temperatures, oxide-mediated spallation coupling is less prominent.
A more homogeneous microstructure reduces the prominence of the proposed spallation mechanism.
Wear-only, corrosion-only, and simultaneous-exposure groups provide a controlled comparison for testing the coupling hypothesis.
Failure to observe excess coupled degradation or a correlation between oxide spallation and accelerated wear and corrosion would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes oxide fragmentation to cyclic sliding stress and phase mismatch, both of which would also be present in the wear-only baseline, yet the baseline is asserted to have a more stable oxide film without identifying how corrosion uniquely destabilizes it.

The prediction compares simultaneous degradation with each isolated baseline, whereas the falsification rule requires it to exceed the sum or an undefined expected synergistic effect. A result could exceed each isolated baseline but not their sum, satisfying the prediction while triggering the stated falsification rule.
